title: Basal-bolus insulin therapy
summary: Basal insulin covers background needs. Bolus insulin covers meals and prescribed corrections.
why: The body needs background insulin even between meals and overnight.
how: Basal insulin helps restrain liver glucose release; mealtime insulin deals with the faster arrival of carbohydrate.
example: During a clinic visit, someone points out which pen has each job in their written plan.
caution: Mixing up basal and bolus insulin can be dangerous. If a mix-up occurs, get urgent professional advice.
question: Can mealtime insulin simply replace the background dose?
answer: They serve different roles. A replacement plan needs a clinician.
takeaways: Learn the names of both insulins
Know whom to call after a mix-up

title: Multiple daily injections (MDI)
summary: MDI delivers insulin by separate injections during the day, typically using a basal and a mealtime preparation.
why: It allows different meals to be covered while maintaining background insulin.
how: Each injection leaves insulin under the skin to absorb according to its formulation.
example: A student keeps the two pens labelled and records injections so a busy timetable does not obscure what was taken.
caution: If a dose may have been missed, use your written instructions or call the team. Guessing can duplicate a dose.
question: Does MDI require a pump?
answer: No. Pens or compatible syringes deliver the injections.
takeaways: A record can help avoid duplication

title: Insulin pens versus syringes
summary: A pen dials a number of units. A syringe draws insulin from a vial using calibrated markings.
why: Choosing a device involves vision, dexterity, training and the exact insulin concentration.
how: Matching a vial to its syringe calibration matters. A pen is designed to deliver its own formulation.
example: At the pharmacy someone checks both the U-40 vial and its matching syringe before accepting a refill.
caution: Never withdraw insulin from a pen with a syringe. Never share a pen even if the needle has been changed.
question: Is the same volume always the same unit count?
answer: No. Units per millilitre depend on the concentration.
takeaways: Keep each pen for one person

title: Insulin pump delivery
summary: A pump delivers insulin through a small cannula or patch at a programmed rate, with boluses for meals.
why: Changing a programmed rate and changing an injected long-acting dose have different effects over time.
how: Most standard pump regimens use rapid-acting insulin for background delivery as well as boluses.
example: Before a trip a pump user asks for a written plan covering loss of the controller or interruption of delivery.
caution: Interrupted delivery can lead to ketones quickly. Keep the backup plan and supplies accessible.
question: Does every pump adjust insulin automatically?
answer: No. Automated delivery also needs a compatible sensor and algorithm.
takeaways: A pump delivers basal and bolus insulin

title: Injection sites
summary: Insulin is injected into the fatty layer under the skin at a suitable site taught by the diabetes team.
why: Areas such as the abdomen, outer thighs, buttocks and selected upper-arm areas differ in access and absorption.
how: Body build, needle length and location affect the chance of reaching muscle. A diabetes nurse can show appropriate boundaries on the actual person.
example: A learner uses the linked injection guide and then demonstrates a site to their educator.
caution: Avoid lumps, scars and damaged skin. Do not infer the right depth or angle from a generic body outline.
question: Where can I see the injection areas?
answer: Open the Diabetes UK injection guide linked below and ask your educator to show the areas suitable for you.

title: Site rotation
summary: Rotation means changing the exact injection spot systematically within the areas approved for you.
why: It reduces repeated trauma to one patch of tissue.
how: A planned sequence within an area makes it easier to leave previous spots to recover. The same favourite spot can become thickened.
example: Someone uses a simple grid on paper and marks the last used area, alternating spots according to their nurse’s instructions.
caution: Moving from lumpy tissue to healthy skin can change absorption. Discuss monitoring and the transition with your team.
question: Does alternating between two tiny spots count as a full rotation?
answer: It still concentrates injections in a small area. Ask for a rotation map that fits your routine.

title: Lipohypertrophy
summary: Lipohypertrophy is a thickened or lumpy area of fat under the skin at repeated insulin sites.
why: It can make insulin absorption less predictable.
how: Repeated exposure to insulin and local tissue trauma can cause changes that are easier to feel than see.
example: At a routine visit the nurse examines a frequently used injection area even though it looks normal.
caution: Avoid injecting into lumps. A change to healthy tissue can increase absorption and the risk of a low.
question: Does a painless favourite spot mean it is a good site?
answer: No. A painless lump should be assessed.
takeaways: Feel as well as look for lumps
Review the transition with the team

title: Injection technique and needle handling
summary: A reliable injection technique delivers insulin using the intended device into subcutaneous tissue.
why: Incomplete delivery, leakage or an incorrect device can change how much insulin reaches the body.
how: The product instructions cover fitting the needle, flow checking, injecting and how long to keep the needle in place.
example: Someone brings their pen to the clinic and demonstrates their routine with a training device.
caution: Use a fresh needle, never share equipment and ask for hands-on teaching. Do not repeat an uncertain dose without advice.
question: Is the hold time identical for every pen?
answer: Follow the instructions for the exact pen.

title: Insulin storage and temperature
summary: Heat, freezing and excessive light can damage insulin. The allowed time after opening depends on the product.
why: Damaged insulin may be less effective even if its appearance seems unchanged.
how: Unopened stock is commonly refrigerated at 2–8°C. In-use temperature limits and discard intervals are specific to the product and device.
example: A family notes the date a pen was opened and checks its leaflet before a hot-weather journey.
caution: Do not use insulin that has frozen. Keep insulin away from freezer plates and direct contact with ice packs.
question: Can appearance prove insulin is still effective?
answer: No. Review storage history and ask a pharmacist about exposed stock.
takeaways: Protect it from heat and freezing

title: Travelling with insulin
summary: Travelling with insulin means protecting the supply from heat, freezing, loss and delays.
why: Checked baggage can be exposed to unsuitable temperatures or separated from the traveller.
how: An insulated carrier can reduce heat exposure. Insulin needs separation from ice or frozen packs.
example: A traveller packs insulin and backup supplies in hand luggage with documentation and original labels.
caution: Check the exact product limits. Ask the team about time-zone changes before departure.
question: Should insulin touch the ice pack inside a cooler?
answer: No. Direct contact can freeze it.

title: Injection discomfort and mistakes
summary: Persistent pain, leakage or bruising is worth discussing during a technique review.
why: Pain can make an already demanding routine harder to maintain.
how: Site choice, repeated needle use and technique can contribute. Reviewing the device in person can identify a fix.
example: A person who dreads injections asks a nurse to watch them use a demonstration pen.
caution: Redness that spreads, warmth, swelling or persistent pain warrants medical assessment.
question: What should I bring to a technique review?
answer: Your own device, needle packaging and a description of where and when the problem occurs.

title: Safe sharps disposal
summary: Used needles and lancets go directly into an appropriate puncture-resistant sharps container.
why: Loose sharps can injure family, cleaners and waste handlers.
how: Keeping the container within reach avoids carrying an exposed sharp around after use.
example: Before leaving the clinic, a family asks where filled containers are accepted locally.
caution: Keep containers away from children. Follow local collection rules and the fill line; loose needles do not belong in recycling.
question: Do all municipalities collect sharps the same way?
answer: No. Ask your clinic, pharmacy or local waste service for the accepted route.
